The Department of Justice has received approval to temporarily stay an order that required it to respond to Apple's document requests directed at 14 federal agencies, as the DOJ appeals an ongoing antitrust lawsuit it has filed against Apple. Here are the details.

先講少少背景

A few weeks ago, Judge Jose Linares, who is presiding over the case, ruled in Apple's favour in a separate lawsuit the company filed seeking documents from 14 federal agencies. That antitrust lawsuit was filed by the DOJ against Apple.

In short, Apple wants these documents to research how the agencies in question evaluate privacy and cybersecurity when making smartphone policy and procurement decisions.

Apple believes the records could support its argument that some of the practices the DOJ is challenging are in fact reasonable product differentiation and security measures, rather than anticompetitive restrictions.

Specifically, Apple is seeking documents from the following agencies:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

Following Judge Linares's ruling in Apple's favour, the DOJ asked him to reconsider. After Linares declined, the DOJ appealed the ruling to District Court Judge Julien Neals, and asked Linares to stay the document production order during the appeal.

Speaking of which, that brings us to the latest development.

DOJ approved to temporarily stay order

In an earlier ruling, Judge Linares granted the DOJ's request to stay the document production order—which concerns whether the government must respond to Apple's document requests—while District Court Judge Julien Neals considers the government's appeal.

Judge Linares said that while he agreed with Apple that the DOJ will have an "uphill battle" to win the appeal, that fact alone was not sufficient grounds to deny the government's request for a stay.

He also agreed with the DOJ's argument that if Judge Neals ultimately overturns his ruling, it would be "manifestly unfair" to first require those 14 agencies to expend the alleged "massive amount of work" responding to Apple's document requests.

In addition, Judge Linares also rejected Apple's argument that staying the order while Judge Neals considers whether to overturn the ruling would cause the company harm by further delaying its access to the documents. He pointed out that the case is still in the "relatively early stages of discovery," and that other discovery work can continue in the meantime.

With the order now stayed, Apple will have an opportunity to respond to the government's appeal, after which the DOJ will have seven calendar days to file a reply. Judge Neals will then decide whether to uphold or overturn Judge Linares's original document production order.
